summary:
Daejeon stands under the legal framework of South Korea, where gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is lawful. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and enforcement has been punitive. In 2017 the military criminally charged 32 personnel in what Amnesty International described as a gay witch hunt, and a gay soldier received a six-month prison sentence for consensual sex. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Daejeon is where the strongest court ruling on trans military status in South Korea was issued. On 7 October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's discharge of the late Staff Sergeant Byun Hee-soo, the first known legal case involving a transgender soldier. The court held that the military should have treated her as female after her legal sex change, that loss of genitalia was not valid grounds for dismissal, and that a fitness review must weigh basic rights. The decision vindicated her posthumous appeal.

The circumstances behind that case remain the sharpest documented harm to a trans person in the country. Staff Sergeant Byun was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a handicap, with gender dysphoria recorded as a mental disorder and a post-surgical physical-disability finding. She died by suicide in March 2021. The Defence Ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty in March 2024, and she was buried at the National Cemetery in Daejeon on 24 June 2024. Some 60 activists attended and protested, arguing that the burial was marred by discriminatory treatment. State burial in Daejeon therefore stands alongside an institutional posture toward transgender personnel that remains restrictive.

Legal gender recognition is available in South Korea and the surgical condition is falling away. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. On 24 November 2022 the Supreme Court ruled en banc that transgender individuals with minor children can have their gender legally recognised provided they are not married, overturning an 11-year-old precedent; a 2011 Supreme Court ruling had required persons seeking gender-affirming care to be over 20, single and without children.

South Korean national law does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and same-sex couples cannot jointly adopt children. A 2024 Constitutional Court ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights is the main advance in that area. No comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTI organisations can register, but an NGO that won registration litigation at the Seoul Metropolitan Court in March 2017 faced government appeals, part of what Human Rights Watch described as years of bureaucratic obstruction.

Restroom access is a live problem in both judicial and school settings. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court ruled final, with no appeal, that police advice telling a trans plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, ordering symbolic compensation of 300,000 won against the state. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, shows trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; a 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reported holding it in and leaving school early, and researchers urged legal and institutional reform.

Healthcare carries an official blind spot identified from within the state itself. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

Documented violence and hostility concentrate at public events and in everyday life. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors and accused police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride some 2,000 police protected 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. A 2014 finding recorded that 54% of LGBTQ Korean youths were harassed by classmates, 16.1% of outed LGBTQ people were recommended conversion therapy, with 65.4% reporting harm and 94% psychological trauma, and a 2018 study found 51.5% of transgender adults faced harsh discrimination in the past year. During the May 2020 Itaewon COVID-19 cluster, contact tracing outed LGBTQ people, doxing and online harassment rose, and a trans-male bartender told NBC News he felt threatened walking on the street absent a nondiscrimination bill.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey published on 27 June 2025 in Epidemiology and Health, covering 585 transgender and non-binary young adults, mapped key milestones and stigmatisation across life stages and documented a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 describes an overall relatively positive record on free media and civil society alongside persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
Daejeon's courts have been more protective of trans status than the military institutions they review. The 7 October 2021 Daejeon District Court judgment treated the Army's dismissal as unlawful on basic-rights grounds, while the Defence Ministry and the military fitness apparatus that produced the 2020 discharge continue to apply a handicap framing to gender-affirming surgery.

The National Cemetery burial of Staff Sergeant Byun on 24 June 2024 sets official honour against lived institutional practice. The state granted line-of-duty recognition in March 2024, yet the roughly 60 activists at the graveside argued the ceremony itself was conducted in a discriminatory manner, and the armed forces retain both the article 92-6 prosecution power and the exclusion of transgender people from service.

Violence risk in South Korea peaks at Pride events rather than in routine movement. Incheon drew an attack by about 1,000 Christian protestors with subsequent charges against pastors and allegations of police inaction, while Busan's 2018 Pride required roughly 2,000 officers to protect 15,000 attendees. Comparable large-city settings, not Daejeon, carry the documented event-level disorder.

Outing by state processes is a recurring channel of harm. The May 2020 Itaewon contact-tracing operation disclosed LGBTQ identities and was followed by doxing and online harassment, and the 2 July 2024 Seoul ruling found that police guidance restricting a trans person's restroom use infringed personal rights.
localsOnly:
Residents can obtain legal gender recognition through the courts, and since the 8 May 2024 ruling the process no longer rests on a surgical precondition; the Supreme Court's 24 November 2022 en banc decision also opened recognition to transgender parents of minor children provided they are unmarried.

Young residents face conscription pressure under a regime that excludes transgender people from military service, while service members remain exposed to Military Criminal Act article 92-6 and its two-year maximum sentence.

Residents have a complaint route through the National Human Rights Commission of Korea, which in November 2023 identified the hospitalisation gap for transgender patients after the Ministry of Health and Welfare declined to write guidelines.

Trans students in Daejeon attend schools where the documented national pattern is restroom avoidance: research presented on 20 March 2024 by the youth centre DDing Dong records trans teenagers holding in and leaving school early rather than risk being outed.

Line-of-duty death can be honoured with burial at the National Cemetery in Daejeon, as in the 24 June 2024 interment of Staff Sergeant Byun Hee-soo, though the ceremony drew organised protest over discriminatory treatment.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Daejeon-specific enforcement figures for Military Criminal Act article 92-6 are sourced; the 32 charges and the six-month sentence date from 2017 military proceedings, and garrison-level activity in this city is not documented in the material available here.

Whether the 7 October 2021 reinstatement of Staff Sergeant Byun Hee-soo produced rank, pension or entitlement consequences is unresolved on the available sources, which record the cancellation of the discharge and the posthumous vindication of the appeal without stating administrative follow-through.

The 24 June 2024 burial account, including the figure of about 60 activists and the claim that the ceremony was marred by discriminatory treatment, rests on a single press report; independent corroboration is not sourced.

Restroom, hate-crime and school-safety figures cited above come from Seoul and national research rather than Daejeon. No local data on restroom access, police response to anti-LGBT incidents, or conversion-therapy referrals in this city is available.

Whether further review of the 2021 Daejeon District Court judgment occurred beyond the posthumous appeal is not stated in the sources.
